# First calls, and the stand-in that makes them free {#sec-ch16}

::: {.epigraph by="Linus Torvalds, Linux kernel mailing list, 2000"}
Talk is cheap. Show me the code.
:::

Every new AI service raises the same practical worries. What does an error look like? Will a bug in a loop cost money? Will my tests break when the network is down? What happens when the provider quietly updates the model?

This chapter answers them for a decision model called through an API. The answers apply to Jev, and to any model you call over the internet.

::: {.goals}
- Swap between a free local stand-in and the real service without changing your logic.
- Tell errors you should retry from errors you should fix, and fit retries to your time limit.
- Decide in advance what a failed call *means*.
- Ask several questions in one call, and know what that saves.
- Record real answers once and replay them in tests.
:::

## One switch decides where the request goes

The official library builds the request, retries failures and turns the response into typed answers. Only its very last step, actually sending the request, talks to the network. That last layer is called the **transport**, and you can swap it.

![The official library does all the work of building requests, retrying and parsing answers. The transport decides where requests go. The book's stand-in answers locally; the default sends them over the network to TypeSafe.](/figures/ch23/layers.pdf){#fig-layers}

The book's stand-in plugs in there (@fig-layers). Your code, the request-building, the retries and the parsing all run exactly as they would for real; only the destination changes. So the stand-in is a faithful copy of the *interface*: same request shape, same answer shape, same error codes. It is not a copy of the *answers*, which come from a small synthetic engine, and every response says so.

That gives you a development pattern worth copying for any paid AI service: build and test everything against a free local stand-in, then flip one switch to go live.

Once live, **fix the model version**. A name like "latest" can point to a new model at any time, and Chapter 9 listed "how behaviour changes between versions" among the true unknowns.

::: {.keyidea}
Fix the model version, so a change in behaviour is your decision, not a surprise.
:::

## Two kinds of error

![The steps of one call. The library checks and sends the request. A success is parsed into typed answers. A rate limit or server error waits and retries. Anything else, or running out of retries, raises an error.](/figures/ch23/lifecycle.pdf){#fig-lifecycle}

Most calls go straight along the top of @fig-lifecycle. The two other paths need opposite treatment.

![What the library does for each kind of failure, measured against the stand-in. Mistakes in your request fail at once. Rate limits and server errors are retried under the default policy.](/figures/ch23/errors.pdf){#fig-errors}

**Your mistakes** fail at once: no key, a model name that doesn't exist, a question with no options. Retrying is pointless; the same request fails the same way. Fix the code.

**Problems outside your code** are worth retrying: rate limits, server errors, a dropped connection. The library retries these twice by default, waiting a little longer each time (@fig-errors).

::: {.keyidea}
Retry errors from outside your code, never your own.
:::

## How many retries?

![The share of calls that succeed as more retries are allowed, when 1%, 5% or 20% of requests fail at random. Dotted lines show the simple formula: a call fails only if every attempt fails.](/figures/ch23/retries.pdf){#fig-retries}

If one request in five fails, only {{< num ch23 ok_20_0 pct >}} of calls succeed with no retries, and {{< num ch23 ok_20_2 pct1 >}} with two (@fig-retries). The arithmetic: if each attempt fails with probability *q*, a call with *r* retries fails with probability *q*^*r*+1^.

But retries cost time: about half a second, then a second. Fine for a background job; useless for a login check with a 300-millisecond budget (Chapter 12).

So treat a failed call as just another case the policy must handle. With a tight time limit, allow no retries and decide what failure *means*. For a login, perhaps "allow, but flag for review". For closing an alert, "don't close; send to a person". Put that rule in the policy, where people can see it, not hidden in a retry setting.

::: {.keyidea}
When time matters, decide in advance what a failed call means.
:::

## Ask together

![Input tokens per call, averaged over 800 alerts, and what they'd cost per million calls at Jev's vendor-reported price. Asking four questions in one call sends the alert once; asking them in four calls sends it four times.](/figures/ch23/tokens.pdf){#fig-tokens}

Four triage questions in one call used about {{< num ch23 tokens_four_one int >}} input tokens; in four separate calls, {{< num ch23 tokens_four_sep int >}}, because the alert was sent four times (@fig-tokens). One call is also one round trip instead of four. And a typical alert is short, about {{< num ch23 tokens_text int >}} tokens, so at the vendor-reported price a million decisions cost a few dollars.

## Tests that never use the network

Tests against the stand-in are already free, fast and repeatable. But eventually you want tests built on *real* answers, without paying for every test run.

![Record once, replay many times. With a key, a recording transport saves each real request and response to a file. In every later test run, a replay transport answers from that file: the same answers, byte for byte, with no key and no cost.](/figures/ch23/record-replay.pdf){#fig-record-replay}

Record real calls once into a file (testers call it a **cassette**), then replay that file in every later run (@fig-record-replay). If a test asks something that wasn't recorded, the replay fails loudly, so a changed question can't slip through. Separately, a scheduled job can call the real service now and then, to check its interface still matches what your code expects.

::: {.breaks}
A stand-in copies the interface, not the model; every answer it gives is synthetic. Some behaviour lives on the server and can only be learned from the real service: exact rate limits, timeouts when it's busy, the exact meaning of its confidence number. Recorded answers go stale, so re-record on a schedule and whenever the model version changes. And retries hide problems as well as fixing them: count them, because a rising retry rate is often the first sign of trouble.
:::

::: {.threshold}
A login check has 300 ms. If the call fails, the login must still be decided. Letting a risky login through costs about \$10,000 × P(attack); blocking an innocent one costs about \$20. A typical login has P(attack) around 0.0001. What should a failed call do?

(With no answer, the best estimate is the base rate. Allowing costs about 0.0001 × \$10,000 = \$1 on average; blocking costs \$20. So allow, and log it for a later check. For a riskier group, such as admin accounts signing in from new countries, the same arithmetic may say: block when the call fails.)
:::

Testing shows your code handles the answers; it can't show the answers are good [@dijkstra1970]. That's what Chapter 11's calibration checks are for.

::: {.exercises}
1. For a service you use, list three errors you'd retry and three you'd fix. What would a failed call *mean* for each decision it makes?
:::
